item.title: Improved Space Bounds for Promise Graph Coloring in Adversarial Streams
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: dynamic stream

Authors: Sergio Thoumi

We study promise graph coloring in one pass insertion-only adversarial streams. We give a randomized algorithm that distinguishes 3-colorable graphs from graphs that are not 6-colorable using $O(n^{3/2}\log(n/\varepsilon)\log n)$ bits of space. This provides a truly subquadratic space algorithm for a constant coloring gap, answering an open problem posed by Assadi, Sundaresan, and Yazdanyar [SODA 2026] for $q=3$. Combining this algorithm with the vertex-sampling lemma of Assadi et al.\ yields, for any $144\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le Q\le n$, a one-pass decision algorithm distinguishing $3$-colorable graphs from graphs that are not $Q$-colorable using $O((n/Q)^{3/2}\log^5 n)$ bits of space. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}((n/Q)^2)$ bound achievable via dynamic streaming techniques. Setting $Q=\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ yields a semi-streaming decision algorithm, answering the decision version of another open problem posed by Assadi et al. On the negative side, we prove that distinguishing $χ(G)\le q$ from $χ(G)\ge(q-1)^2$ requires $Ω(n^2/q^5)$ bits of space, improving upon the previously established $q^2/4$ threshold using the same space complexity.

item.title:
TR26-264 | On Testing Finite Groups |
Nader Bshouty
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Let $G=[n]$ and let an unknown binary operation $*:G\times G\to G$ be given by oracle access to its multiplication table. The tester is given $n$ explicitly as part of its input. A query chooses $x,y\in G$ and receives $x*y$. We study randomized adaptive two-sided property testers for deciding whether $(G,*)$ is a group. An input is considered far from the property if one must change at least an $\epsilon$-fraction of the $n^2$ table entries in order to obtain any group operation on the same labeled set. We prove three results. First, there is a tester using $$O\left(n+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries and $\tilde O\left(n+1/\epsilon\right)$ time. In fact, this tester has one-sided error. This improve the Goldreich-Tauber tester~\cite{GoldreichTauber25}, that uses $\tilde O(n/\epsilon)$ queries. Second, if computational efficiency is ignored, a dictionary-and-locator construction combined with an action-consistency test on an expanding Cayley graph gives a tester using $$\tilde O\left(\sqrt{\frac n\epsilon}+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries. This is the first query complexity bound for this problem that is sublinear in $n$. Third, there are infinitely many values of $n$ for which every adaptive randomized two-sided tester needs $$\Omega \left(n^{1/5}+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries. This improves on the $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound of Goldreich and Tauber. The lower bound uses two randomly relabeled abelian groups of almost equal orders, embeds them into multiplication tables on the same $n$-element set, and couples arbitrary adaptive query transcripts.

item.title:
TR26-265 | Near-Optimal Bounds for Testing Residual-String Equality and Parenthesis Languages |
Hadar Strauss
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Residual-String Equality, denoted $\text{ResStringEq}$, is the property consisting of all pairs of strings over $\{0,1,*\}$ that are equal after deleting all `$*$' symbols from them. This property was first introduced by Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA 2018), who used it to show a lower bound on testing the $\text{Dyck}$ languages, where $\text{Dyck}_m$ is the language consisting of balanced sequences of parentheses over $m$ parenthesis types. They showed that testing $\text{ResStringEq}$ on inputs of length $n$ requires $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ queries, and presented a reduction from testing $\text{ResStringEq}$ to testing $\text{Dyck}_m$ for any $m \geq 2$. Furthermore, they showed that $\text{Dyck}_m$ can be tested with $O(n^{2/5+\delta})$ queries for every constant proximity parameter, where $\delta>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. In this work, we nearly close the gap, by showing that testing $\text{ResStringEq}$, and hence $\text{Dyck}_m$ (for any $m\geq 2$), requires $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ queries. We also show a stronger lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for testers that make non-adaptive queries. We establish that the $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ bound is nearly tight, by presenting a non-adaptive tester for $\text{ResStringEq}$ that uses $O(n^{1/2+\delta})$ queries for an arbitrarily small constant $\delta>0$. Furthermore, we extend this non-adaptive tester to the $\text{Dyck}$ languages, with the same query complexity. Finally, we improve the dependence on the proximity parameter $\epsilon$ in the tester of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya, reducing it from $O(1/\epsilon)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\delta)}$ to $O(1/\epsilon)^{O(\log(1/\delta))}$.

item.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: maximum matching

Authors: Quanlong Niu, Riheng Jia

The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.

item.title: How to Walk a Dog in Parallel: On Parallel Computation of the Discrete Frechet Distance
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Leonid Barenboim, Arnold Filtser, Omrit Filtser, Orr Fischer

The Fréchet distance (also known as the dog-leash distance) is a well-studied and prevalent distance measure for polygonal curves. In this paper we present parallel algorithms for computing the discrete \frechet\ distance between two curves, in both the PRAM and MPC models. For two polygonal curves of length $n$, we show that the distance between them can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log n/ σ)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+σ})$ total work for any $0<σ<1$. In the sublinear MPC model with $n^ρ$ space per machine, it can be computed in $O(\log n / ρ^2)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+ρ})$ total space. For $c$-packed curves, we match our bounds to the sequential algorithms, showing that a $(1+\eps)$-approximation of the distance can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log{n}+1/σ^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+σ})$ total work, and in the sublinear MPC model in $O(1 /ρ^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+ρ})$ total space, for any constant $\eps>0$. As part of our algorithms for $c$-packed curves, we also present parallel algorithms for computing curve simplifications, which may be of independent interest.

item.title: Zero Knowledge for Free up to Linear Query Bounds: Quasilinear-Size Constant-Query Zero-Knowledge PCPs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Inhyuk Park, Chenglin Fan

We show that for all polynomials $T$ and $b$, every relation in NTIME($T$) has a binary PCP with $O(1)$ non-adaptive queries, perfect completeness, soundness error 1/2 and length $(T+b)\cdot(\log(T+b))^{O(1)}$, which is perfect zero knowledge against every adaptive, possibly malicious verifier making at most $b$ queries. This improves the length $\tilde O(T+b^2)$ of Zeilberger, O'Connor, Gur and Spooner (2026), who observed that Dinur's gap amplification preserves zero knowledge. The simulator runs in expected polynomial time (or in strict polynomial time, with a failure symbol or with negligible statistical error). For $b\le T$ the length is $T\cdot\mathrm{polylog}\,T$, the form of the shortest known constant-query PCPs without zero knowledge. Unless NP $\subseteq$ BPP, the dependence on $b$ is optimal up to the polylogarithmic factor for polynomial-time simulators: zero knowledge is free up to linear query bounds. Zero-knowledge interactive oracle proofs achieved length $\tilde O(T+b)$ in 2016-17; we obtain it for PCPs. Gur, O'Connor and Spooner (STOC 2025) asked whether NP has such PCPs of quasilinear length (their Open Problem 1). This paper answers it for every polynomial query bound, with the simulators above in place of a strict polynomial-time perfect simulator. The proofs were developed with extensive AI assistance and have been checked by the authors. We mask the Reed-Solomon proof of proximity of Ben-Sasson and Sudan at every node of its recursion. By a locator lemma, at every node, whatever $k$ of its proof symbols reveal about its input is determined by $O(k)$ input values. We prove it with the coprime-order argument of Bafna and Vyas (2026); our treatment of domain points is new. Dinur's gap amplification gives constant query complexity. The query count and the polylogarithmic exponent are absolute but very large.

item.title:
TR26-268 | A Linear Lower Bound on Testing Graph Isomorphism in the Bounded-Degree Model |
Amit Dror
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

We prove a linear query complexity lower bound for two-sided testing of graph isomorphism in the bounded-degree model. Specifically, there are constants $d$ and $\varepsilon_0$ such that, for every sufficiently large $n$, there exists an $n$-vertex graph $H_n$ of maximum degree at most $d$ such that testing isomorphism to $H_n$ requires $\Omega(n)$ queries. The proof proceeds by a reduction from testing the solvability of a fixed sparse system of linear equations over $\mathcal{F}_2$. Given a fixed matrix $A$ and an input vector $b$, we associate $b$ with a graph $G_b$ such that $G_b$ is isomorphic to $G_0$ whenever $Ax=b$ has a solution. We show that each query to the graph can be emulated with at most one query to $b$, and that Hamming distance from $Im(A)$ translates to the distance of $G_b$ from $G_0$. The main result then follows from a linear query lower bound for testing the solvability of the underlying (sparse) linear system.

item.title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Timothé Picavet

We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is $d+1+\varepsilon$, which is optimal up to $\varepsilon$ for every even integer $d\geq 2$. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and $(5+\varepsilon)$-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the $7+\varepsilon$ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to $\varepsilon$. Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on $1/\varepsilon$ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

item.title: Kempe Reachability with $k\geq 3$ Colors Is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-Complete on Claw-Free Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: vertex coloring

Authors: Duc A. Hoang

A \emph{proper vertex coloring} assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices have distinct colors. A \emph{Kempe change} in a proper vertex coloring exchanges two colors on one component of the subgraph induced by the vertices of those colors. For a fixed palette of $k$ colors, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} asks whether two given proper vertex colorings of the same graph are connected by a sequence of Kempe changes. This problem is known to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. A graph is \emph{claw-free} if no vertex has three pairwise nonadjacent neighbors. The \emph{line graph} of a graph has one vertex for each edge, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges share an end. Line graphs are claw-free, and their Kempe changes correspond to \emph{edge-Kempe changes} in the original graph, which exchange two colors on one component of the subgraph formed by the edges of those colors. A claw-free graph with a proper $k$-coloring has maximum degree at most $2k-2$, whereas for $k\geq 4$ all proper $k$-colorings of a graph of maximum degree at most $k$ are connected by Kempe changes. We show that, for every fixed $k\geq 3$, \textsc{Kempe Reachability} with $k$ colors is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on line graphs of connected simple $k$-regular graphs, and hence even on connected $(2k-2)$-regular claw-free graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether two proper $k$-edge-colorings are connected by edge-Kempe changes is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even on connected simple $k$-regular graphs. ChatGPT 6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to assist with developing and reviewing mathematical arguments and drafting and revising the paper. The author takes full responsibility for the correctness and content of the paper.

item.title: No Perfect Randomized Composition
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Alexander Meiburg

Does computing a composition of total Boolean functions require the product of the randomized query complexities of its factors? We give a negative answer. There are families of total functions $f,g$ such that $R(f\circ g) =Θ\!\left(\frac1{\log R(g)}\right)R(f)R(g)$ This result requires first separating linearized query complexity $\LR$, as well as noisy randomized query complexity $noisyR$, from standard randomized query complexity $R$. Both constructions essentially come from totalizing existing partial function separations, albeit via different techniques. By adapting these techniques, we also construct total functions separating every adjacent pair in the chain from sabotage $RS$, max-conflict $\barχ$, and linearised query complexity $LR$. We show that AND-of-ORs separates conflict $χ$ from max-conflict $\barχ$ complexity and makes conflict and sabotage incomparable. Finally, randomized complexity can be smaller than its composition limit $R^*$ by the maximal factor $Θ(\log R)$. The total--total composition separation is also formalized in Lean.

item.title:
TR26-269 | Settling Nondeterministic Communication Complexity of Graph Connectivity |
Zhijun Zhang
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Determining the communication complexity of graph connectivity has been one of the longest standing open problems in communication complexity since the seminal work of Babai, Frankl, and Simon [FOCS'86]. A simple protocol transmits a spanning forest using $O(N\log N)$ communication on $N$-vertex graphs. While this was shown optimal for deterministic protocols by Hajnal, Maass, and Turán [STOC'88], the optimal nondeterministic and randomized complexities have remained unresolved for decades. We settle the nondeterministic communication complexity of graph connectivity by proving an optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bound. The best prior bound was $\Omega(N\log\log N)$ due to Raz and Spieker [Combinatorica'95]. Our bound is shown by upper bounding the maximum size of $1$-monochromatic rectangles. Generalizing our techniques to weighted, almost $1$-monochromatic rectangles yields an $\Omega(N \cdot \log(\min(1/\varepsilon,N)))$ lower bound for randomized protocols with error probability $\varepsilon$. In particular, this bound is optimal for any polynomially small $\varepsilon$. For constant error probability, we also prove that any $r$-round protocol requires $\Omega(N/r \cdot \log N)$ communication, which is optimal for every constant $r$. Previously, optimal $\Omega(N\log N)$ lower bounds for graph connectivity were known only for $1$-round [Sun, Woodruff; APPROX/RANDOM'15] and $2$-round protocols [Radhakrishnan, Reddy, Venkat; ITCS'26]. Our proof introduces a new communication problem which can be viewed as a composition of inner product and pointer chasing problems. Our lower bounds can be extended to other fundamental graph properties, and also imply optimality of known query and streaming algorithms for related problems.

item.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Niels Inselmann Christiansen, Eva Rotenberg

We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in some biconnected graph G in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries of the form "are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between a and b?". All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. All queries and updates are answered in worst-case $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get an algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case running time of $O(\log^2 n)$ per operation. These algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.

item.title: A Nearly Optimal Min-Cut Algorithm for Dynamic Streams
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: dynamic stream

Authors: Yang P. Liu, Hoai-An Nguyen, Vihan Shah, David P. Woodruff

We give an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space algorithm for the minimum cut problem in dynamic streams, resolving the space complexity of streaming min-cut up to polylogarithmic factors. Ding, Garces, Li, Lin, Nelson, Shah, and Woodruff (ITCS 2025) obtained the same $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$ space bound for insertion-only streams, while prior to our work the best known bound even for unweighted dynamic streams was $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$, due to Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS 2012). Our main technical contribution is an $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-space for-each cut sketch in dynamic streams, which may be of independent interest. The construction applies to weighted graphs under general $\pmΔ$ updates, a stronger model than the standard dynamic-stream setting in which weighted edges are inserted and deleted in their entirety. Despite this stronger guarantee, our algorithm is surprisingly simple and relies on very little machinery. We also obtain applications to minimum $\ell_p$-norm $k$-partitioning for every fixed $k$, weighted correlation-clustering evaluation for two clusters, and for-each cut sketching in balanced directed graphs.

item.title: When is greedy exact for weighted minimum 3-cut?
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Armando Rodado Amaris

The greedy algorithm for minimum 3-cut splits a global minimum-weight cut and then the cheaper of its two sides; it is a tight $4/3$-approximation. We show that it is exact, from every global minimum-weight cut, whenever some optimal 3-partition has two parts joined by total weight at least the weighted edge connectivity $λ$. This extends both theorems of Hochbaum and Shmoys from unweighted planar graphs to all weighted graphs, recovers the $4/3$ bound, and generalizes to minimum $k$-cut with a one-paragraph proof. The remaining hard instances have all pair weights below $λ$; for them we prove a merge lemma for Gomory-Hu sides. Finally, we give a 7-vertex graph with a unique Gomory-Hu tree whose unique optimal 3-partition contains no side of that tree, so the first stage of Kapoor's algorithm does not suffice on its own. The main theorem, the 4/3 bound, the merge lemmas and the counterexample are verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

item.title: Extrinsic Curvature Estimation by Closest Point Projection of Rays
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: neighbor query

Authors: Liangchen Liu, Yen-Hsi Richard Tsai

We propose a parametrization-free framework for estimating the second fundamental form and the principal curvatures of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The method uses the closest point projections of a few short random rays and recovers the curvature from the curves that these projections induce on the submanifold, without coordinate charts or local fitting. We analyze the geometry of the induced curves and characterize when they are geodesics. For hypersurfaces, these results give two algorithms with error bounds: a least squares reconstruction of the second fundamental form from the curvatures of the induced curves, and a direct estimate of all principal curvatures from the eigenvalues of a $d\times d$ matrix built from $d$ rays, which needs no normal information and costs $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ besides the projections. In higher codimension, we can also recover the second fundamental form one normal direction at a time. On point clouds, where the projection becomes a nearest neighbor query, we bound the additional error. Experiments confirm the predicted rates for hypersurfaces in up to $128$ dimensions, for surfaces of codimension up to $98$, and on point clouds, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in practice.
